To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we isolated by 5' and 3' RACE from a murine (mouse) brain cDNA library a composite cDNA sequence that encodes a putative G protein coupled receptor.

the novel gene encodes a G-protein-couple receptor, that the gene is expressed in many tissues and cell types, and that the gene is a member of a family of genes that have been shown to be important in the regulation of immune and inflammatory responses.
a putative GPCR was isolated from mouse and that the gene is widely expressed.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the isolation and molecular characterization of a putative murine G-protein-couple receptor.
the characterization of a novel murine gene encoding a putative G protein-coupled receptor, which is widely expressed in the mouse.
the molecular characterization of a novel putative G-proteincoupled receptor, the expression of which is regulated at the level of transcription.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the murine putative receptor is widely expressed in many tissues, and that it is a potential candidate for a G-protein-couple receptor.
the murine G-protein-couple receptor gene encodes a protein with 91.5 % amino acid identity to its human counterpart.
this receptor is expressed in a variety of tissues and is a potential candidate for a wide range of physiological functions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we isolated a putative G-coupled receptor from a murine cDNA library.
we have isolated the murine ortholog of the recently identified human GPR37, which has been shown to be a novel G-protein-couple receptor.
this receptor, which we named GPR37, may be involved in the regulation and/or modulation of the function of the central nervous system, the immune system, and the reproductive system.

the GPCR gene family is a large and diverse one, and that there are many more GPCR genes that have not been identified yet.
